boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Natural Bridge record (March 6, 1865) in Operations near Saint Mark's [March 1865]. The March 4-5 skirmishes at the East River and Newport bridges and the naval operations off St. Marks are context. Campaign-wide marches, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen US force text names the 2nd and 99th U.S. Colored Infantry without a figure; the frozen CS text lists local units and 'reinforcements from Georgia amounting to approx. 1,000 men', with a frozen CS bound of 1,000. The live field reads zero. Newton's March 15 report gives his force as 900 to 1,000 men with two navy howitzers and a captured 12-pounder, and the enemy 'it is said' 1,500 to 2,000; his March 19 report gives 893 enlisted men and a prisoner's statement of 1,500 to 2,000. His April 6 letter says he had only 500 men in line when over 1,000 veterans arrived from Georgia, and puts the Confederate total at over 2,000; his April 19 letter says the enemy was over 1,000 at first and was reinforced by 1,000, and that the enemy's available force when the expedition started did not exceed 700. His April 17 postscript lists the Confederate units named in a Tallahassee newspaper and adds that it omits over 1,000 Georgia reinforcements.
claims.rationale: One commander's successive estimates, several secondhand, for different moments of the day. The frozen CS text appears to follow Newton's postscript list (its units occur in his list in the same order, his list adding cadets, the Second Florida Cavalry and Scott's battalion; Georgia reinforcements of about 1,000 against his 'over 1,000'); its basis is not stated in any inspected passage. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Newton says the Confederates held intrenchments at the bridge with sloughs, ponds, marshes and thickets in front and on the flanks; Townsend's flanking attempt was stopped by a wide, deep slough; his own position was a low salient in the marshes under cross-fire, and he withdrew 300 yards to open pine barrens. He adds that the bridge could have been held by 200 resolute men and that the approach road proved over eight miles long rather than the four or five the guides promised.
claims.rationale: Ground described by an interested commander; no map verification. The Confederate works were in place when the attack came.

claims.value: Newton's plan was to march to Newport, cross the St. Marks, take St. Marks in rear or strike the railroad to Tallahassee, while the navy silenced the batteries and landed 500 to 600 seamen at Port Leon. His April letters describe it as a raid meant to occupy the enemy nearer home, deter attacks on the southern forts and divert forces from Steele's column. NPS says the aim was to engage and destroy the Confederates who had attacked Cedar Keys and Fort Myers.
claims.rationale: Stated plan and later statements of purpose by one commander; the later framing is partly self-justifying.

claims.value: Newton directed Major Lincoln's assault on the bridge, Colonel Townsend's attempt on the Confederate right and Pearsall's support, then decided to withdraw to the pine barrens; he blames the navy's failure, which he connects with the relief of its commander after he landed. He names Generals Jones and Miller as the Confederate commanders. The frozen commanders are Major General John Newton (US) and Major General Sam Jones (CS); Newton signs these reports as brigadier general, and the live page gives Samuel Jones without rank.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the Union commander only; no listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. NPS says the Union troops, unable to take the bridge, retreated to the fleet. Newton reports the complete repulse of two Confederate charges, leaving him master of the field, and a withdrawal in order because the navy could not ascend the river.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Newton's claim to have held the field is his own.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 174 (US 148; CS 26); the live field reads 173 (US 148; CS 25). Newton's March 15 report gave 150 killed, wounded and missing; his March 19 report and casualty table give 148, of whom 35 missing (the table's total row is garbled in OCR). He gives no Confederate figure.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: No Confederate report is printed with these operations in Official Records I, XLIX part 1; Sam Jones's and William Miller's reports, if any, remain unlocated. Weeks's report, the inclosed Jones order and newspaper extract, Gibson's letter and the naval reports in Official Records of the Navies I, 17 remain deferred.
No history covering Natural Bridge was found in this pass; Samuel Jones's Siege of Charleston ends in 1863.

NPS/CWSAC (NPS battle page and frozen Arnold rows) is one family. John Newton's reports of March 15 and 19 and April 6, 17 and 19, 1865 and his casualty report (Official Records I, XLIX part 1) are one family of interested and partly self-justifying Union accounts; two families (NPS and Newton) are recorded as the effort ceiling. Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
